en: Oṃ, homage to the Three Jewels!

Even today, the forest-like groves of the lotus-faces of Māra’s daughters shrink back as if at the rays of the moon— the songs of his former lives of heroic deeds, so difficult to perform, which are sung by the beautiful women of the gods and *kiṃnaras*.
He, whose body was charming with good fortune, who was most wonderful, whose sight was difficult for those of meager merit to obtain,
and who fulfilled the heart's desires of the world he favored— his sole activity was the essence of altruism, like a wish-fulfilling gem.
He who always became one whose sole essence was the happiness of others, and through the suffering of others experienced supreme suffering himself;
he, whose quality of great compassion was so intensely established that his own pain and pleasure were entirely set aside—of him [I speak].
O Vicchinna, you who caused the head of one [to fall] for the sake of another, that very head attained the state of a lotus by being offered;
yet for your own sake, the earth became like the sharpened edge of a sword, with its white parasol shattered.

By him, who delighted in benefiting the world, whose emergence was manifest, who was radiant with virtues, and who shattered the darkness of faults—by him, as by a charming moon that has risen, the world was illuminated. (Śl_5)

His auspicious teaching, which possesses unbroken and pure conduct like a crest-ornament set with the finest jewels, dispels the darkness of dissolution at the summit of the netherworld, borne upon the massive heads of the serpents.
Like a cloud of Dharma risen for the benefit of others, he rained down the nectar of the Dharma, which is like water of a single flavor;
yet, through its manifold applications, it extinguishes the various fevers of suffering.
In vessels that are wide, deep, stainless, clearly manifest, and capable of enduring all friction, whatever is placed therein serves the benefit of all people... [and so forth].
Those who do not attain, nor drink, nor uphold that vigilance which removes death, birth, and old age— they,
being possessed by the great intoxication of abundant delusion, are crushed by the mountain of Dharma.

That they abandon delusion after having fully realized that teaching— which is the one stainless eye common to the entire world and the sole lamp of the three realms— is the manifestation of the Supreme Wonder.

Placing their steps upon the rungs of the staircase to the palace of enlightenment as if they were already well-known, they proceed along the lofty path without turning back; yet, when they turn back, they descend to their own original ground.
Who in this world would cast away the raft of ethical discipline already within their grasp, desiring to cross the ocean of birth which is so exceedingly difficult to traverse?
How could one who has fallen into the midst of a wilderness, having strayed from the noble caravan and being ignorant of the good path, not grieve for a long time?
Those who, intent on rising from the abyss within the mountain caves of saṃsāra and from the supreme darkness,
cast aside the garland of the Victor’s qualities along the way, fall with speed into a treacherous precipice below.

Even when alone, those who, having established a discipline in their minds, uplift themselves through the accumulation of action—those virtuous ones become the crowns of the circle of the world; by them alone do true teachers attain the status of being "gurus" through their excellent disciples.
Having obtained the noble lady— who, like a mother, gives birth to a flood of virtues— and following her whose heart is exceedingly pure,
those radiant ones, devoted to abiding in truth, would rather abandon their very lives with ease than their promise.
Let alone all the slanders of the people here, and all the paths of evil and the terrible hells;
when this [reputation] instantly abandons one's innate nature, what greater suffering for a virtuous person could there be on earth than that?
He who, having reached the vast path composed of Dharma prepared by the sages, abandons it like one who has boarded a ship only to leave it behind—
his mind is made restless by a longing for the dancing of the revolutions within the ocean of saṃsāra, despite his observance of restraints.
He who, mounted upon the wheel of saṃsāra that revolves incessantly, experiences pleasure while it is turning,
will inevitably, driven by the force of karma, gradually traverse all the states of existence, both favorable and unfavorable.

Having entered the womb-abode— which is obstructed by a mass of impurities of most foul odor, extremely cramped, and filled with dense darkness— just like a hell, he endures great suffering with his limbs huddled together.
Then, by the course of time, as if being squeezed by a press of solid oil, he somehow reaches the earth;
yet even so, that he does not immediately abandon his life is solely due to the difficulty of finding a state where such suffering can be experienced.
Remaining there in that impurity, revolving within it with his body enveloped by the moist *kalala*, and emitting a great and pungent stench,
he— being tormented as if by loathing— abandons it like a burst wound of former memories when its foul humors have reached suppuration.
Having abandoned childhood—its every refinement lost, its limbs slack and disordered—one becomes devoid of being;
yet, due to delusion, one wallows in the caves on the slopes of the lofty mountains of youth, which are abodes of the poison of sensory perceptions.
From that state as well, he falls unconscious; yet even having fallen, he does not abandon his agitation.
Thus the fool continues to imagine his own body to be graceful, ageless, and immortal.
Abandoning the excellent path frequented by the lords of sages, he wanders on a wrong path, deluded;
like an elephant in rut, unrestrained and acting with impetuosity, he tramples everything else to pieces.
Then, as if an elephant-driver were acting upon an elephant, Old Age— placing her feet mercilessly upon his head against his will— forces upon him the sharp goad of gray hair.
Nevertheless, though his conduct is crooked and he has abandoned virtue out of fear and the like,
he performs good deeds while deluded, like a flowering arrow aimed at his own destruction.
Then Antaka, as if laughing with his floods of grey hair and his fierce glances,
proceeds to swallow him upon the head— the disease of old age, whose pacification is impossible.
Then his joints break apart, his intellect departs, and his state of being declines;
his body goes to ruin, yet the hope for life certainly increases all the more.
And gradually, with his senses closed and his power destroyed, though still longing for sense-objects,
he reaches that state which he undergoes in hell— if that state is indeed terrifying.
"How was this done by me? How was it not done? Alas, my course is ruined!
How was it that I did not notice this enemy as he placed his foot upon my head? (Śloka 30)
Thus, his mind afflicted by mental agonies born of evil deeds and filled with sorrow,
he was gazed upon with compassion by his kinsmen, who were themselves stricken with sickness and shedding tears.
With its vital points and joints violently tormented, as if entering a most terrible darkness,
it abandons its own beloved body, which had been protected with great effort.
With his hair seized and bound by firm nooses, he wails, held fast by the messengers of Yama;
yet people do not hear his speech, being distracted by their own cries of lamentation.
On paths difficult to traverse due to spreading rocks, mountains, and rivers, and crowded with exceedingly sharp thorns,
he is dragged along by the terrible agents of Death, struck by the staff of Yama, while the noose of Time is fastened around his neck.
When one who is intensely thirsty approaches, having seen from afar that which appears to be pure water,
it turns out to be a flow of blood— stained with the mire of putrid pus and mixed with the moss of a mass of hair— yet it is perceived as water.
Malaya, whose peaks are cooled by spray tossed by the sea breeze and which possesses dark sandalwood trees, may he travel to;
yet even that mountain becomes jagged with heaps of extinguished embers, licked and shattered by the rows of flames from fierce forest fires.
If he goes to the ocean, which possesses a loud laughter of foam produced by the breaking of fierce and tossing waves,
even that [ocean] becomes like a harsh wind for him, blowing through clouds of heated, white, and dreadful sandbanks.

As he stands there, foretelling the arrival of the clouds, the bearer of water pours upon his body a rain of iron arrows— consisting of embers, smoke, thunderbolts, and sparks, and tinged with the reddish-gold hue of streaks of lightning.
To one afflicted by heat, even a beneficial breeze produces burning; to one afflicted by cold, even fire produces coolness.
To one deluded by the ripening of extremely fierce karma, this entire universe then appears as its opposite.
For the needle-mouthed one, whose belly is many yojanas wide and terrifying, even as he drinks water from the great ocean in his state of distress,
every drop of water reaches his broad throat only to be utterly consumed by the heat of the phlegm falling into its cavernous depths.
And [the hungry ghost] has his limbs crushed and pulverized by the thunderbolt-like tips of the fangs of a pack of snarling, massive dogs.
On the banks of the Vaitaraṇī river, filled with caustic water, one is dragged across jagged rocks sharpened to a hundred million points.
Running with great speed through forests of sword-leaves where his body is severed upon beds of sharpened razors,
he falls helpless into a pit— the mouth of Death, conquered by sharp spears, javelins, darts, swords, and maces.
With his body exhausted and tormented by the unbearable heat of the scorching sun, he approaches the trees with their thick, dark green leaves;
yet, his form pierced by the falling hundreds of leaf-weapons, he remains there for a long time, crying out with no one else as his kinsman.
He is embraced by women whose ornaments blaze, crowded with hundreds of sparks issuing from their tips,
and who, though their bodies are as harsh as saws, embrace him mercilessly out of inner love.
With his entire body pulverized and shattered by the collision with herds of rams as terrifying and formidable as mountains,
and his life-breath snatched away by the coldness of a gust of wind, he is likewise crushed again into hundreds of pieces.
Terrified by thousands of screaming swords and jackals, he again ascends those fierce [trees] with rapid strides,
his body pierced by a mass of downward-pointing thorns of that Kūṭa-śālmali tree, leaving him with deep-seated shafts.
Tightly bound by the coils of Time, which are like the nooses of Death slipped from its very hand— coils that are venomous serpents with raised hoods—
the crane, the crow, the vulture, and the falcon forcibly tear out the quivering eyes of one who remains there.

With their mouths resembling the tips of thunderbolts, they forcibly rend his body while he lies asleep; with his form pierced by many thick, sharp iron spikes pointing upward, he descends, deprived of consciousness and uttering cries of distress.
Some there, their bodies pierced by flaming spikes and sharp arrows, being unable to descend from that very place,
have their entrails and sinews torn apart as they are dragged by fierce, sharpened iron weapons with jagged edges.
Some fall upon the rugged slopes of mountains; some enter the interior of boiling oil-pans that have been dragged along;
others, unable to find a place to set their feet, enter a ground of heated sand strewn with flying sparks.

Others, however, their bodies putrid with urine and shattered by swarms of tiny, wriggling creatures, are unable to move even so much as a step; they live on, their lives bound by the noose made of karma.
Even their bones, being carried away by a wind beyond compare for its coldness, caused their limbs to become withered, trembling, and shriveled;
they were covered with erupting and bursting pustules, and from their wounds, which were being devoured by hundreds of insects, flowed marrow, fat, and lymph.
With their teeth clenched together and their hair and body-hair standing on end, their eyes, ears, and throats constricted and pierced by pain,
they remain in the cold hells with bodies that have reached a state of extreme numbness, crying out intensely.
The atmosphere was turned smoky by the scattered, vast, and fierce stench of pungent smoke; the circle of the quarters was made formidable by the mass of spreading flames acting as hands;
adorned with heaps of white bones and skulls, the terrifying and horrific scene unfolded like Bhairava himself, brandishing a human-skin garment amidst cries of "Hā! Hā!"
In some places, filled with large sparks flashing *caṭacchaḍhat*, and in others, momentarily suppressing its expansion with the sound *chamacchamat* within the fat;
and in the cavities of the unstable chest, it falls with a *kaṭatkaṭat* ringing, a hellish fire that has surpassed the fire at the end of an aeon.

With their ribs scorched by the fire of withered, ancient grass, their tongues flickering and emitting blazing flames, they are terrified by the protruding entrails streaming from their burst bellies; their only remaining activity is the emission of heavy, gurgling sounds.
Having repeatedly observed an opening in the abyss from afar, those who seek refuge from the suffering of delusion somehow proceed toward it;
yet when even that is blocked by the firm bands of karma, their desires rendered fruitless, they go once more to some other state of misery.

Following the rain of showers from blazing, sharp javelins, those struck by the staffs of the hell-wardens drink molten iron, which is wreathed in garlands of fiery rays; with blood trickling from their mouths, ears, and nostrils, they emit columns of smoke through these very apertures.
With the mass of his tawny flames ignited by the brains from their skulls and eyes, which were scorched and split open,
he approaches those heaps of limbs like a pit of the fire of grief, mercilessly consuming them as if they were a pile of dry fuel.
Those creatures, whose lives are as unstable as the waters of mountain torrents, find that very same parching heat in the hells and those very same fires;
indeed, their own actions transform everything in such a way that it appears utterly and most cruelly terrifying.
For a being who has somehow escaped from hell— the abode of evil— after being helplessly entangled by the snare of his own karma,
human birth is indeed extremely difficult to attain amidst the worlds that are agitated by the fear of infinite varieties of rebirth.
If he should take birth among the Mlecchas who share the same vows as the guardians of hell, or among the animals that devour one another,
he will practice that very same conduct there by which he falls once again into the abyss.

Having attained that which carries one to the further shore even of the ocean of birth, which plants the seed of supreme enlightenment for the sake of auspiciousness, and which surpasses even the wish-fulfilling gem in its abundance of virtues—what person here would render this human state fruitless? (Śloka 63)
Having attained this human state which is exceedingly difficult to find, one should accomplish exactly that which is desired;
for there is no certainty of stability even for a single moment in a lifespan that flickers like the flame of a lamp tossed by a violent wind.

While people are thinking, "This task must be done tomorrow," or "This other one today," or "This in a moment," or "This in an instant," I suspect that the impatient and enraged Kṛtānta laughs, his staff of Time stained yellow by his sidelong glances.

"This arrival of flowers has come with blossoming blooms; this autumn, adorned with the moon as its tilaka, has arrived"—at these words, everyone rejoices, yet my life departs into supreme despondency, for it is now exhausted.

In mountain peaks and forest glades where the moon’s orb serves as a nearby ornament, where the girdle of heavy water-bearing clouds rests, and where all attachments have ceased, the fortunate spend their lives, whose nature is as flickering as the wind.
Is that delight found upon the grounds of the Nandana grove, on the stone slabs of the hips of celestial maidens,
which is found rather in forest regions— frequented by groups of most charming young women, free from attachment, and exquisitely beautiful?
Was that delight found in the celestial rivers with their pure waters and secluded, lovely banks, which spread the fragrance of blooming *saṃtānaka* blossoms,
that was found in the forest streams?
The vast caves of the mountains—delightful because they are free from the bustle of people, possessing deep expanses, and encircled by streaks of green forest;
situated near riverbanks and inaccessible due to the sweet, humming sounds of bees in their solitude—seem to say to travelers, "This is the fire of affliction."

Desires and women have been declared by the Jina to be like illusions, mirages, the moon reflected in water, and waves; yet fools, deceived by the delusions that are as fleeting as those found within a dream, fall into the hells to which they remain attached.
Sense objects are like poison, sweet only at first encounter; sense objects are like poison, bitter in their ultimate consequence.
Sense objects are like poison, dense with the darkness of delusion; sense objects are like poison, as fickle and impetuous as an irresistible torrent.
When desires and sense objects are examined, poison is better than sense objects, for sense objects are by nature poisonous.
Poison becomes poisonous in a single lifetime, whereas sense objects remain poisonous even in future births.
Poison and sense objects have very different spheres of influence:
poison kills when it is consumed, whereas sense objects kill even from mere recollection.
Poison mixed with poison attains pacification when treated by those who hold antidotes and employ effective mantras;
or even poison, when properly administered, may be for the benefit of men. But the great poison of the sense-objects is never like this.
Just as a bull, having climbed to the edge of an uneven pit, falls into the abyss with a mind longing for a mere blade of young durva grass—
yet that very fall is his gain— so too is this world of living beings, whose minds are possessed by pleasure.
Having enjoyed playful excursions with the Apsarases, their tresses disheveled by the currents of the Mandākinī,
they wander once more upon the harsh Vaitaraṇī river, enduring terrible suffering as their bodies are shattered by contact with its waves.
Having sported in the celestial groves with their beloveds upon carpets spread of the sprouts of the Kalpa-trees,
they wander once again through the plains of the Sword-Leaf Forest (Asipattravana), where their limbs are severed by the falling of sharp and agitated weapons.
Having wandered for a long time upon the slopes of Mount Meru, where the ground rises and falls with pleasant sensations to the touch,
they wander on with their feet, thighs, and arms scorched by heaps of blazing sand, hot ashes, and fire.
Having gone to heaven in celestial chariots bristling with clusters of pearl necklaces and rows of tinkling, radiant bells,
they fall once more headlong into the dense, bottomless, and shoreless darkness below— a place of terrible and fixed abode.

Even Śakra, whose footstool is made tawny by the mass of light from the crests of gods, *kiṃnaras*, *nāgas*, and *yakṣas*, goes to a miserable state when his course is agitated by the wind of karma; what man indeed would not feel fear in such a situation?

With their flowers withered, their bodies smeared with [blood], their garments faded, and their circle of kinsmen initiated into the rite of grief, the gods undergo a supreme suffering at the time of death; yet humans—whose lives are as flickering as water bubbles—do not.
In this world, which is terrifying due to the obstruction of the raging fire of suffering, people maintain a conceit of happiness;
yet that is the wide-open mouth of Death, and the very seed of the tree of rebirth once again.
Bound by the firm and long threads of the nature of craving, with the terrifying staff of Time cast down and aimed at it,
this is like a fishhook set by Death for sentient beings who are tossed about in the ocean of existence.
Having raised their necks for a moment from the violent surge of heat within the thick, boiling mire of the Kumbhīpāka hell, and having found the release of a sigh of relief, the denizens of hell—
though being struck by many iron mallets filled with fury— regard that very state as supreme happiness.
In the same way, being incessantly and helplessly tormented by dreadful sufferings for so long a time, and having somehow escaped the agitation of the fires of old age and hell,
when his own unbearable fire of suffering has momentarily subsided, the whole world develops a thirst for a mere village of fragments of bodily pleasure.
To the extent that the notion of happiness arises in the entire world, to that same extent the fire of passion increases with ever more flames;
to the extent that the cultivation of the beautiful is practiced, to that same extent the darkness of delusion becomes increasingly dense.
To the extent that the meditation on the foul steadily increases,
to that same extent the blinding darkness of delusion becomes increasingly more unstable.

When poets compare the limbs of women to the lotus, the moon, and the blue water-lily—despite their being foul-smelling, putrid, and distorted—the terrible fruit of that falsehood is this: they enter into those very same things as their place of abode within the womb.
What destiny in this world has not been traversed hundreds of times? What pleasure has not been experienced repeatedly in the past?
What those splendors have not been attained, whose charming smiles are like flickering chowries? And yet, passion continues to increase.
There are no rivers whose sands he has not enjoyed; there is no place in the world where he has not made his dwelling;
nor is there any spot in the sky that he has not traversed. Yet, insatiable as it is, passion continues to grow.
There is no suffering that has not been experienced repeatedly in the past; there are no sensual pleasures in this world through which one has not found satisfaction;
and there is no sentient being who has not lain within a womb. Since all this is so, how can detachment arise?

In this vast world, as one undergoes birth and repeatedly revolves through many states of suffering and happiness, there is no person in the world who has not been a kinsman; yet even so, the serpent of hatred remains with its terrifying coils.
With whom I have come together to laugh, to sport, to sing, and to eat and drink in one place; with whom I have held conversations;
and how many delightful years have been spent in the course of time—some of them easy, others difficult—I have somehow passed through all these various conditions.
Beholding them— straightforward yet vanishing in the turn of their speed, as if fallen into the midst of a whirlpool—
if one abandons these kinsmen who have entered the ocean of saṃsāra and departs alone, then there is no such thing as an ungrateful person.

Who indeed— even a bandit— would venture to abandon those women whose breast-milk, followed by affection, was drunk by helpless infants held upon their laps, while they themselves were the sole recipients of abundant and fruitless indulgence?

Who indeed—even an enemy—would venture to depart from this body, leaving behind those who, though confined within the belly and provided with space there, carried it so loosely with minds softened by affection; those now suffering, helpless, and miserable?

In this world scattered by floods of suffering, helpless and without refuge, the virtuous call that suffering which is endured for the sake of others true happiness. Even those who find momentary delight in the cessation of hunger, thirst, heat, and fatigue—having made the welfare of others their supreme goal—who indeed in this world could be their equal?
Neither by means of excellent pleasures, nor by the trappings of royal splendor, nor by wives, nor by children, nor in the abode of the gods, nor in the realm of the asuras,
do those devoted to enjoyment ever attain that sensual happiness which those dedicated to establishing the welfare and happiness of others obtain in some measure.
Even a beast eats fodder that is easily obtained by itself, or drinks water when parched with thirst, having found it by chance;
but if this man here strives to accomplish the welfare of another, that is his own true splendor—this indeed is happiness, this is true manliness!

When the sun, with its tireless horses, wanders about creating light, and when the earth, bearing an incalculable burden, maintains constant light—this is not for any self-interest; rather, this is simply the nature of the great: that they find their sole delight in the singular essence of the welfare and happiness of the world.
Beholding the world fallen helplessly into the blazing fire of suffering, enveloped by the confused wandering of the blind smoke of ignorance,
those wonderful persons who here proceed with their heads as if wrapped in the flickering flames of that fire are truly the virtuous ones.
With their hair standing on end, they plunge into the Avīci hell, though it is filled with the flames of fire and cool as a mass of snow or the rays of the moon;
for the sake of others, this very lotus pond—though its smile is the blooming lotuses—causes them distress like a dense cluster of fire-flames.
The virtuous, girding their loins for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others, dwell happily even in the Forest of Sword-leaves;
they do not, however, take delight for even a moment in the Nandana grove, accompanied by the beauties of the gods.
Having crossed over themselves, these steadfast ones cross the Vaitaraṇī river once again in order to ferry across the people who have no refuge;
yet they do not personally indulge in the pleasure of contact with the shifting play of the waves of the celestial river.

Thus, worship this jewel of good conduct— the ornament of ornaments, auspicious and immortal, noble and radiant among the radiant, difficult for the ungrateful to obtain, the delight of those who rejoice, the cause of equal happiness, and the most auspicious of all blessings.
The flower of the Sugata’s word should always be cultivated; like the flowers of trees, it bears a magnificent fruit.
From the flower of the Sugata’s word, a mass of meaning is to be gathered by those who, like bees, have an intense longing for its honey.
Abandon the objects of the senses, which are crowded with worldly affairs and perish in an instant; resort instead to that equanimity which is free from longing and devoid of the fear of Death.
Dispel the darkness of delusion and remove the bolt of its deception; for noble young horses do not indeed sleep for very long.

With the Vinaya as its spreading branches, the aggregate of vigor as its trunk, patience and self-restraint as its sprouts, tranquility as its flowers, wisdom as its boughs, and generosity as its thick canopy;
with aspiration as its peak, ethical conduct as its shade, and bestowing the fruit of perfect peace—be you the one great tree for those suffering from the heat in the desert of existence!
O you who bring benefit to many, with the great roar of your speech, the vast torrential downpour of your purification, impelled by the wind of compassion;
you who have stilled the dust and adorned the earth with the shade of your virtue—be you the one great cloud for those suffering from the heat in the desert of worldly existence!

Manifestly vast, with bottomless mud yet a most serene foundation, perpetually cool, and free from the danger of lurking serpents; naturally beautiful, capable of enduring the crushing weight of cutting off craving—be you the one great lake for those tormented by the heat in the desert!

Whatever merit has been acquired by me through reciting this account of the Sugata’s life, may all people, having placed their faith in it, become perpetually happy, possessing delightful enjoyments and fulfilled aspirations; and, delighting in the welfare of others, may they gradually attain omniscience.

May the hells possess a vast splendor, their surfaces as level as the palms of hands, clearly illuminated, with their fires extinguished; covered by the leaves of land-lotuses, bristling with sprouts of lotus-fibers, pure and fragrant, their grounds adorned with blooming lotuses, and accompanied by breezes laden with spray.

May the desired arisings of Buddhas occur in every direction at all times— those who have conquered the armies of Māra with their cries of victory, who have proclaimed the sound of fearlessness, whose delightful play in the waters of the sky is shared by men and gods alike, and who destroy the continuous succession of the afflictions of birth, death, and exhaustion.
May there be for the worlds the fragrance of Dharma, a great festival of literary compositions; may the desires of Death remain barren for a long time;
and may the auspicious light of the moon, rendered perpetually cool by the continuous rains of the gatherings of sages and Janakas engaged in conversation, attain its ultimate fulfillment.
Thus ends the religious poem titled *Śiṣyalekha*.
The work of the venerable master Candragomin.
